title: Basic Sentence Correction
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Finding and fixing common errors in sentences

introduction.overview: Sentence correction asks you to find the error in a sentence or to choose the correct version from several options. The errors in basic questions fall into a small number of families: subject-verb agreement, wrong tense or verb form, wrong preposition, wrong article, wrong pronoun case, adjective used for an adverb, double comparatives, and unnecessary words. A systematic approach is to read the sentence once for meaning, then check it against a short list of error types.
introduction.placementRelevance: Sentence correction and error-spotting items are commonly asked in the verbal ability section of company aptitude rounds. They draw on all the earlier grammar chapters, so they are a good test of how well those topics have been learned.
introduction.realWorldContext: Proofreading emails, resumes and reports before sending uses the same checklist: agreement, tense, prepositions, articles, pronouns.

learningObjectives: Apply an error-checklist to any sentence
Spot subject-verb disagreement, wrong tense and wrong verb forms
Spot wrong prepositions, articles, pronoun cases and adjective/adverb confusions
Recognise double comparatives, unnecessary words and wrong word order in reported questions
Choose the grammatically correct and natural option

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Keep the earlier rules ready: the verb agrees with its subject; since + point, for + period; prefer to; articles by sound; object pronouns after prepositions; adjectives modify nouns, adverbs modify verbs.

coreDefinitions: Error spotting: finding the part of a sentence that is grammatically wrong.
Sentence improvement: choosing the best replacement for an underlined part.
Double comparative: using both more and -er (more smarter), which is wrong.
Reported question: a question reported indirectly, which takes statement word order (She asked where I lived).
Redundancy: using two words that mean the same (return back, repeat again).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Most errors fall into the same ten or so families. Instead of searching blindly for a mistake, run the sentence through a checklist. After a few weeks of practice, the checklist becomes automatic and you can spot the error almost on first reading.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Read the sentence once. Underline the subject and the verb and ask whether they agree. Check the tense against any time word. Check each preposition and article. Check the pronouns. Finally check for extra words. Most sentences fail on one of these tests.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Agreement check
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Ignore phrases between the subject and the verb.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Verb-form check
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: After did/does/do and modals use the base form; after has/have/had use the past participle

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Adjective/adverb check
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Verbs take adverbs (sings well, runs fast); linking verbs take adjectives (looks good)
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Good is an adjective; well is an adverb.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Comparison check
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Use either -er or more, not both; use "than", not "then"
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: He is smarter than his brother

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Reported speech check
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: No "that" before a reported question; use statement word order
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: She asked me where I lived.

mainNarrative: Begin with agreement. "She don't like tea" fails because the singular subject she needs the singular auxiliary doesn't. "Each of the boys have a book" fails because the real subject is each (singular), so has is needed. "The furniture are old" fails because furniture is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

Next check the verb forms and tenses. After do, does or did the main verb stays in the base form: "He did not come yesterday." After has, have or had the verb takes the past participle: "He has gone." Time words such as yesterday, ago and last year need the simple past: "I saw him yesterday".

Then check the small words. Prepositions follow fixed patterns: prefer to, look forward to meeting, in spite of the rain (or despite the rain), agree with someone (no "am agree"). Articles depend on sound: an MBA, a university.

Adjectives and adverbs: "She sings very good" is wrong because sings (a verb) needs the adverb well. "More smarter" is a double comparative; use smarter or more intelligent. Do not write "than" as "then" in comparisons.

Reported questions use statement order and no "that": "She asked me where I lived" (not "She asked me that where I lived"). Use told with an object (She told me) and said without one (She said that...). Avoid redundancy such as "return back" and "repeat again".

deepDiveAspects.title: "The reason is because"
deepDiveAspects.content: The reason is that something happened; because already means "for the reason that", so "the reason is because" is redundant. Write "The reason is that he was late".

deepDiveAspects.title: "Look forward to" takes -ing
deepDiveAspects.content: In the phrase look forward to, to is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or -ing form: "I look forward to meeting you" (not "to meet you"). The same applies to "be used to" and "object to".

problemVariations.description: Subject and verb do not match.
problemVariations.exampleSnippet: Each of the boys have a book.
She asked me that where I lived.

solvedExamples.title: Agreement and auxiliary
solvedExamples.question: Find the error: "She don't like tea."
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: The singular third-person subject needs the singular auxiliary.

steps.title: Identify subject and verb
steps.explanation: The subject is "she"; the auxiliary is "don't".

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Do/does must agree with the subject.

solvedExamples.title: Verb form after did
solvedExamples.question: Find the error: "He did not came yesterday."
givenInfo: Sentence: He did not came yesterday.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: After did not, the main verb is in the base form.

steps.title: Spot the auxiliary
steps.explanation: "Did not" already shows the past tense.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The tense is carried by "did", so the main verb stays in its base form.

solvedExamples.title: Reported question
solvedExamples.question: Find the error: "She asked me that where I lived."
givenInfo: Sentence: She asked me that where I lived.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: A reported question takes statement word order and no "that".

steps.title: Spot the extra word
steps.explanation: "That" is not used before a reported question.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: She asked me where I lived.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: A reported question is joined by the question word itself.

shortcutMethods.title: Checklist of ten

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Read and reread the sentence until something feels wrong.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Check in this order: subject-verb agreement, tense and verb form, preposition, article, pronoun, adjective/adverb, comparison, reported speech, redundancy, word order. Most errors appear in the first four.

rulesForApplication: Strike out phrases between the subject and the verb before checking agreement.
After do/does/did and modals use the base verb.
Look forward to + -ing; prefer to; in spite of / despite (no "of" after despite).
Good is an adjective, well is an adverb.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Reading for "feel" rather than for rules.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Use the checklist in a fixed order.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Changing a correct part and leaving the real error.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Find the error type first, then fix only that part.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing an option that is correct but changes the meaning
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Picking a grammatically correct sentence with a different meaning.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Check the meaning against the original.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming that every sentence has an error.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: If the checklist finds nothing, the sentence is correct.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Compare the options; the part that differs is usually where the error lies.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Do these after finishing easier verbal items; apply the checklist consistently.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Because the same ten error types recur, practice gives rapid gains in speed.

summaryBullets: After did/does/do and modals, use the base form.
No double comparatives; than not then.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I fix "He did not came yesterday"?
Can I explain why "more smarter" is wrong?
Can I turn "She asked me that where I lived" into a correct sentence?
